TOO COLD TO CAMP. . . 



. . . but not to talk about! 


Even early campers can start forest fires which kill wildlife 
and pollute fishing waters. Each year, more than 500 forest 
fires in Ontario are traced to careless vacationers who fail to 
extinguish their camp fires and smokes.

THE GAP 


FOR THE SAKE OF ARGUMENT 


IS GETTING WIDER 


We are all of us acquainted with the 
less attractive symptoms of advancing 
years which manifest themselves in 
stairs getting steeper, print getting 
smaller and clothes being made skim¬ 
pier around the waistline. If you are 
a camp director, you have probably 
also noticed that stafF arc getting 
younger, while you, on the other hand, 
are getting older—often as much as 
two or three years at a time. This is 
one of the facts of life which, while 
not as fascinating to hear about as the 
birds and the bees, is nonetheless facing 
all of us who have been camping for 
any length of time. 

When I Was a Counsellor 

“When I was a counsellor ...” We 
know, we know—you worked 24 hours 
a day for a mere pittance, you hacked 
down balsam boughs to make a bed 
instead of inflating an air mattress. You 
slaved for hours over Mulligan stew 
on a trip instead of adding water and 
stirring. You paddled for hours, and 
hours against strong head winds every 
day of a six-day trip instead of being 
towed or trucked to the nearest por¬ 
tage. You slept in a leaky tent with 
nothing but an old orange crate to hold 
your clothes. And you talked easily of 
words like integrity, honour and re¬ 
sponsibility and virtue and you believed 
that hard work and dedication would 
eventually bring you out on top. 

So here you are—out on top—and 
ready to pass on to new generations the 
love of camping and the out-of-doors 


which so coloured your childhood. You 
still believe in honour and integrity and 
responsibility and virtue and you are 
determined to give the children of to¬ 
day the same fierce pride in hard work 
that you had. 

And what happens? You find that 
the world you knew as a child has gone, 
never to return, and that the rewards 
of hard work and dedication seem to 
come just as easily to those who have 
shown no evidence of either. 

To-day’s counsellor besides being a 
great deal younger than we were at the 
time, is a very different sort of person. 
Not having grown up in a depression 
he or she has very little idea of the real 
value of money. It is there to be spent 
—let’s spend it! All counsellors -ask for 
more money now, usually with the ex¬ 
planation that they must pay for col¬ 
lege. How odd it is then to find at the 
end of the summer that so much of that 
salary has already been spent—on days 
off, for clothes, expensive meals, trips, 
long-distance calls, car repairs. 

Young Staff 

Young staff are FREE. Even in high 
school there is unprecedented freedom, 
and college discipline, or lack of it, is 
a matter for great concern. The 
eighteen year-old who has had a year at 
college is used to coming and going as 
he likes with very few restrictions. 

Most of our staff are too young. A 
counsellor, who on a bitterly windy 


30 


Canadian Camping 





cold morning arrives to breakfast wear¬ 
ing two sweaters, wool slacks and ski 
mitts accompanied by her campers in 
shorts and sleeveless blouses is too 
young to be in charge of children. The 
counsellor who complains because her 
ten-year olds act like children, dawd¬ 
ling and wasting time and giggling at 
nothing, is too young herself to have 
any understanding of age cliaracteris- 
tics. The girl who is “a wonderful 
baby-sitter” (and which of us does not 
have at least three such on our staff?) 
hasn’t got the maturity of judgment to 
enable her to stay calm on a sleep-out 
with her campers when things start to 
go bump in the night. 

Well, you say, my Senior Staff are 
excellent people. My Section Heads 
are supposed to cope with problems of 
immaturity like this. But how old are 
our Section Heads and Senior Staff? 
Most of them are second-year college 
students, worried about the pressure of 
courses, troubled by the new morality 
and their own lapses, in revolt against 
their parents and the authority of The 
Establishment, unwilling to wait and 
work for things they want, scornful of 
religion and resentful of any suggestion 
that some people deserve more privi¬ 
leges because they have worked for 
them. They want to stay out too late 
at night, go too far on a day off, spend 
too much money on food and drink, 
and turn a deaf ear to the Director’s 
plea that they get enough sleep to do 
a good job the next day. In most cases 
they also turn a deaf ear to the Direc¬ 
tor who points out the dishonesty of 
taking a job and the money which goes 
with it and then proving too tired or 
emotionally upset to do the job ade¬ 
quately. We know that it is dishonest; 
they think we are squares. 

As Camp Directors 

As camp directors we are appalled 
at the taste in literature which comes 
to camp — often sent by well-meaning 


parents. True Romance, Teen Age 
Horror, Life and Love — these are often 
supplemented by ones much more lurid. 
Pooh and Alice and Paddington Bear 
have a difficult time holding their own 
when many of these books filter down 
to Intermediate and Junior camp. 
Camp Directors need the help of ma¬ 
ture self-adequate counsellors to cope 
with this type of thing. But so often 
these same counsellors are too im¬ 
mersed in their own problems. Or else 
they assume the role of a Junior Freud 
and take on their own totally inade¬ 
quate shoulders the responsibilities of a 
trained psychologist. 

Perhaps at your camp you have 
some traditions, passed down from year 
to year, basically unchanged since the 
camp was started. They may be a little 
bit corny — but corny or not they call 
forth a tremendous upsurge of loyalty 
from campers and former staff mem¬ 
bers. Plow do we get these across to 
new staff — people who have come to 
us from other camps who already have 
a loyalty to other traditions — some 
who are new and have no conception 
of camp life at all? How do we im¬ 
mediately make them feel that “this is 
my camp”? Schools and colleges have 
so much longer. Camps have two or 
four or eight weeks. 

We don’t know half the things our 
staff knows. I sit amazed sometimes 
at the talk which goes on when staff 
get together. Nuclear fission, existen- 



W inter, 1968 


31 



tialism, churches without God, com¬ 
puter sciences, the world of space. I 
feel like a back number when they 
start in, and yet I cannot rid myself of 
the sneaking feeling of relief that I 
don’t have to know all that in order to 
pass an exam; and that I don’t have to 
cope with New Maths when, according 
to my accountant, I haven’t even mas¬ 
tered the Old! 

In many ways, my stafT make me 
feel inadequate, too. When I was young 
and thoughtless, I didn’t get all worked 
up about the Negro, the under-privi- 
lcdged, the war in Viet Nam or the 
United appeal. Not for me the protest 
marches, the money drives, the sit-in 
strikes. They have a feeling for hu¬ 
manity these young people, that you 
and I lacked. There is a tremendous 
loyalty among them, too, which often 
makes a Camp Director’s life harder 
than it needs to be. (Just try getting 
to the bottom of any rumour or situa¬ 
tion which is causing dissension among 
your staff!). They have an independent 
spirit which I like, too. They go off 
for a year to Europe; they take jobs at 
the ends of the earth in order to see the 
world, make money and get away from 
home. Thousands of them leave com¬ 
fortable, affluent homes in order to 
work, often without pay or recognition, 
for the downtrodden peoples of the 
world. (How sad it then makes you to 
see them settle for a humdrum job with 
a big company which offers a big 
pension! ) 

A Harder Job 

But this independence and freedom 
for counsellors makes a director’s job 
harder than it was years ago. Coun¬ 
sellors used to stay with one Camp for 
three or four summers as a general 
counsellor then finally assume a posi¬ 
tion of importance and responsibility 
as a Section Plead or Activity Head. 


Now, in order to keep these young 
people, we must advance them both 
money-wise and position-wise (and 
aren’t those deadly phrases?) every 
yea i' whether they are really old enough 
or not. If we don’t, some other camp 
will, and we are left starting all over 
again with the seventeen year-olds. 

What do we do? Do we throw up 
our hands and sell our camps for real 
estate and take a nice quiet job in a 
boiler factory? Do we throw our own 
standards and values out with the bath¬ 
water and run our camps the way our 
20 year old counsellors want us to? Do 
we bang our heads against the wall and 
do it “the old fashioned way” losing 
our staff each year to someone who is 
more “broad-minded”? Or do we try 
to walk the razor’s edge between now 
and twenty years ago and work out a 
compromise? 

Our Confederation is changing. Our 
social mores are changing. So, too, are 
the churches and education. Camp di¬ 
rectors must go along with this change 
or be left behind. 

None of us has all the answers. One 
camp has a Counsellor Council which 
decides matters of curfew, drinking, 
smoking, time-off and staff recreation. 
Another camp has year-round meetings 
of senior staff' to discuss problems and 
decide on solutions before they actually 
happen. Some camps hire a psychia¬ 
trist and psychologist for counsellors 
as well as campers. Another gives 
counsellors a say in camp policy and 
still another pays a system of dividends 
after a successful (financial only) sum¬ 
mer. All these things have value, but 
they are not the ultimate answer if 
camps are still to offer to children and 


32 


Canadian Camping 


young adults the magic which they are 
in such a unique position to do. 

Camp directors are still free — free 
to run the type of camp according 
to the dictates of their own heart and 
understanding. Unlike the schools we 
have relatively little governmental in¬ 
terference, and we are still the most 
important person in that camp (say 
what you like about cooks . . . and who 
doesn’t!) We are the people who must 
decide what type of camp we will run 
and we are the ones who must decide 
what type of people we will hire to 
help us run it. They are not easy to 
find now — for camps must compete 
against so many other things for a 
young person’s interest. But having 
found them we must not let their influ¬ 
ence, through lack of time or uncer¬ 
tainty on our own part, become useless 
and inadequate. Young counsellors 
have thrown out many of the standards 
which we had, but I am convinced that 
they arc still looking for the fences that 
you and I used to hurl ourselves 
against. We wanted freedom too, but 
we wanted to know that the boundaries 
were still there. All modern evidence 
to the contrary I suggest that young 
counsellors still feel much the same. 
They want some standards, they want 
boundaries, they want to feel that some¬ 
one cares whether or not they come up 
to expectations. We cannot go all the 
way — if we did we would forfeit the 
position which age, experience and 
(hopefully) maturity have given us. We 
can go half way, and if camps are to 
continue to play a major role in the 
education of the child and the young 
adult, we must go half way. 

Do you agree with the authors? If not, 
how about telling us why?

AT EXPO 

International 

Camping 

Day 


HEADS CAMPING ASSOCIATION: Mrs. 
Nicholas D. Demetelin, new president of the 
Quebec Camping Association , with Howard 
G. Gibbs, left, national director of program 
services , Boys Clubs of America, and Doug¬ 
las G. McEwen, president of the Canadian 
Camping Association. Mr. Gibbs addressed 
a luncheon marking International Camping 
Day at Expo. 


Saturday, September 23, 1967 was 
an exciting day for the Quebec Camp¬ 
ing Association Inc. - Association Des 
Camps Du Quebec Inc. for that was 
the date set for the long anticipated 
International Camping Day at Expo. 
The theme was “The Camper and His 
World - Terre des Jeunes” and at the 
luncheon Mr. Howard G. Gibbs of 
New York stimulated and inspired 
his audience with his pertinent and 
astringent observations. 

As National Director of Program 
Services of the Boys’ Clubs of America, 
Mr. Gibbs speaks with authority. 
Among other things he said that 
present day society is robbing children 
of their childhood because “we want 
them to be adults”. 

He defined schooling as any serious 
undertaking as opposed to clinical 
recreation and enjoyment. 


by Sophia Demetelin, 

President, 

Quebec Camping Association Inc. 


Mr. Gibbs said the new trend, 
spawned from the “sputnik syndrome” 
which influenced North America into 
thinking that we arc far behind the 
Soviet Union in education, is a direct 
cause of the numerous school drop-outs 
and “hippies”. 

Ironically, the more we push our 
children, the more will they fall away 
from school. 

He challenged the various camping 
associations throughout the continent 
to launch a new approach in attracting 
parents and children, to show them 
that the “pseudo-intellectual” idea 
about pushing children into adulthood 
is not in the best interest. 

The camping day observance also 
included a meeting of the Pro¬ 
vincial Board of the Quebec Camp¬ 
ing Association. New officers are 
Mrs. Nicholas D. Demetelin, president; 
Robert Lazanik, A. Ross Seaman and 
Reverend Lionel Perras, vice-presi¬ 
dents; Paul Moreau, secretary; and 
Tony Shorgan, past president. 

— • 


34 


Canadian Camping 



_ CHARCOAL 

== FIRE 

==s FOOD 


reprinted from 

The Canadian Guide, February 1966 


As every Guide must know by now, 
“practice” Heritage Camps have been 
held in many parts of Canada. 

Guide leaders and Guides have 
learned a lot about their camping skills 
at these Heritage Gamps, and one of 
the things they’ve learned is that most 
of us need practice in charcoal cooking. 

Now, there’s no point in waiting to 
learn about outdoor cooking (and most 
of it is done with charcoal now) until 
you get to camp. 

You want to have these skills before 
you go to camp. So why not start 
practising some charcoal cooking now? 

In winter? Sure, why not? What’s 
better than hot food cooked outdoors 
after a skating party or a sleighride? 

So, read these hints, study the draw¬ 
ings — and then why don’t you ask 
Captain to help you organize a com¬ 
pany outing and find the equipment to 
practice some charcoal cooking? 

Timing 

You must plan the time at which 
you want to eat, and then you must 
decide when to start the charcoal burn¬ 
ing and when to start cooking. 


Give charcoal a good half hour after 
you light it to burn down to a bed ol 
rich glowing coals good for cooking. 
In thirty minutes you’ll have a good 
fire for boiling and frying: if you plan 
to broil the food, let the coals burn 
down a little longer. And if you’re 
going to toast something, like hot dog 
rolls or bread, wait until there’s a lot 
of ash. 

Then, when you want to heat water 
for dishes, scrape the ash away and let 
the coals get red-hot once again. 

Tinder 

You can use bundles of cedar bark, 
spruce needles, pine cones or wood 
shavings, heaping the charcoal on top. 

You shouldn’t use any liquid or 
chemical “firestarter” out of a store- 
bought can because this can be 
dangerous. But, if you think there 
won’t be enough natural tinder around 
the site, use one of these things: 

— Waxed milk cartons. You can put 
the charcoal in the cartons and set 
them alight, or you can shred up the 
cartons and heap the charcoal on top. 


Winter , 1968 


35 








—Firebugs, which you make at 
home ahead of time. Roll up four or 
five sheets of newspaper and tie them 
with string every two inches. Then 
cut the roll between strings, dip each 
piece in melted paraffin and let it 
harden. Two or three of these will 
ignite a pile of charcoal. (See diagram.) 



—Buddy Burners, which you also 
make at home ahead of time. Coil 
strips of corrugated cardboard into 
a small salmon can (with the top 
removed). Add a wick, then pour 
melted paraffin or used candles all 
over, and let it harden. (See diagram.) 



— Egg cartons. Fill them with char¬ 
coal, tie them with string so the char¬ 
coal doesn’t spill in your knapsack, 
and set them alight in the stove. 

The Stove 

Some charcoal stoves have a metal 
collar to keep the charcoal confined 


■as it ignites. You can make one out 
of a big juice can with the top and 
bottom removed. Cut ventilation holes 
at the bottom and punch holes 
throughout. (See diagram.) 



Put tinder and charcoal in the can, 
and ignite. When the charcoal is 
burning merrily, use tongs to lift away 
the can and spread out the charcoal. 

Tinder and charcoal need lots of air 
to burn. 

Clean Up 

Put the dish water on to heat as soon 
as the cooking’s done. 

When the outing’s over, get together 
with the rest of the patrol or company 
and ask yourselves how r well you did. 

Were the fires started in good time? 
Was the cooking well organized, and 
were the cooks free to eat with every¬ 
one else? Was the dishwater ready, 
and were the pots soaked during the 
meal? Did you dirty too many 
utensils? Did you remember to dunk 
partly-burnt charcoal in water and 
save it for next time? 


36 


Canadian Camping 






































BOVS CAMP / 


by Muriel Leeson, 
Winnipeg, Man. 


When a mother sends her only son, 
or her eldest son, to Boys’ Camp for 
the first time, it is a sight to make a 
strong man bang his head on the wall. 

Her first act is to supplement the 
clothing requirements recommended by 
the Camp Directors. 

“How.” she reasons, as women have 
reasoned from the dawn of time, “can 
a bunch of men and boys know what a 
boy needs?” (The only woman in the 
place is the nurse whom, for some 
reason, she trusts. Few boys are sent 
to Camp with shots of penicillin or 
bundles of Band-Aids.) 

Extra Luggage 

Consequently, son is dispatched with 
extra shirts, underwear, pants, etc., 
that either get lost or come home 
unused. The things he has worn come 
back in a condition beyond description 
and are generally lugged down to the 
basement in one horrible bundle held 
at arm’s length. It is at this point that 
a woman discovers a boy is quite 
capable of bringing home four pairs 
of si/e eight socks — he has lost the 
other two pair — and one lone, worn 
size ten sock with a hole in the toe. 
How it got in his baggage or why it 
remained there is forever a mystery. 
He certainly doesn’t know. He was 
too busy being a boy. And anyway, 
he was against taking all that stuff in 
the first place. 

FI is attitude confirms Mother’s 
opinion — one long suspected after ten 
years of living with Dad — that deep- 
rooted in every male is a strong aver¬ 


sion to baggage of any kind. When man 
roamed the forests, club in hand, any 
woman who meekly suggested they 
bring an extra sleeping skin probably 
got hit on the head! In a way this 
aversion is a good thing. Today’s male, 
weighed down with a station wagon 
full of gear and a highchair and two 
knocked-down cribs strapped to the 
top, is in no state to conquer the 
world. He will be lucky to get out of 
the car door with both eyes. By then 
he is usually too furious to see, anyway. 

Packing 

The most deadly Mother and Son 
packing battles are held over warmth. 
Mother, being particularly fierce on 
this point, generally wins and son 
goes burdened with the extra blanket. 
If the weather turns cold and he uses 
it, it is never mentioned. On returning 
home he dumps it down, messy and 
damp, with his other gear and removes 
himself. If, however, a warm spell has 
made it superfluous he hollers about it 
loudly and with gestures, not only 
then but again next year at packing 
time. 

“I never used it. It kept falling oiT 
my bed! I don’t need it!” 

Like Little Black Sambo he will 
think in terms of the last time, when 
it was warm, even if a cold air mass 
is approaching with the speed of light. 

This aversion to baggage shows itself 
in other ways. Men are awfully loose- 
minded about lists. Boys’ Camps 
require the clothing lists to be checked 
o(T weekly. (It says this in the letter.) 
Mothers soon find out that this check 
is done by a squirrel, called in for the 
purpose while the men of the camp go 
off on a hike. The nurse will go home 
with her own bathing suit, undies and 
hair curlers, but the boys will be lucky 
if they return with their own heads. 
I once heard of a mother who, to prove 


Winter, 1968 


37 


the squirrel theory, inserted on her 
list, TWO PAIRS OF DINOSAURS. 
They came back checked. 

Forms and Mail 

There is always a Personal Informa¬ 
tion section on the application form, 
insisted upon by a woman higher up 
the scale than the man who runs the 
Camp. In this section Mother is urged 
to tell what she knows about her boy 
in order to help the leaders give him a 
happy camping experience. Ha! No 
mother worth her salt does much about 
that. A boy will have enough trouble 
in life without mother running ahead 
like a herald, telling what she knows 
about him. A good mother lets him 
have an unhappy camping experience 
if necessary but she keeps those facts 
under her hat. This is a low trick to 
play on a boy and any man knows it. 
The Cabin Counsellor will find out 
about little Willie’s unique personality 
the same way Mother did. And he’ll 
re-mould him in one quarter the time, 
in a man’s way. When a boy can’t 
appeal to mother he sharpens up fast. 
By the time a letter gets home he will 
have made six more bloopers so why 
bother? 

In regard to mail, Camp Directors 
urge Mother to write often, keep the 
letters light, bright and happy, but 
never tell Willie what he’s missing. In 
other words, if Uncle Jack blows into 
town and treats the rest of the clan 
to fried chicken and a night at the 
circus, wait until Willie comes home to 
inform him. The note may arrive on 
the day he is having his first attack of 
homesickness and this will put the lid 
on it. He may have begged for six 
months to go to this camp but home¬ 
sick people aren’t reasonable. 

When he emerges from this phase 
(and he will) he’ll begin to see some 
of the more obvious advantages of 
Camp life. For example, at Camp, 
under certain conditions, the Chief can 


be heaved, fully clothed, into the pool. 
He can also be hit in the face with a 
custard pie. These things are always 
a bust with Mother. At Camp a boy 
can paint himself all colors of the rain¬ 
bow at stunt time, get as muddy as he 
likes and yell at the top of his lungs. 
And if an itsy-bit of red paint like 
eight square inches gets on his pillow¬ 
case that night the Cabin Counsellor 
won’t beef. In short, Camp is a 
rewarding experience. 

Don’t expect to hear about it in his 
letters, however. You might, if the lad 
is a future journalist, but more typical 
is something like this. 

“Dear Mom and Dad, 

My filling just fell out while 
eating that toffe. I don’t no what 
to do. Send me a letter telling me 
what to do. 

Your son,” 

The answer to that is tell him to for¬ 
get it, unless it aches. In that case, tell 
the nurse. The Camp authorities will 
take it from there. 

The Big Tiling 

The big thing in sending a boy to 
Camp is to trust the folks in charge 
and remember that in spite of Mothers 
efforts to prevent them, they are trying 
to turn Willie into a Man. In defiance 
of Mothers who fuddle-duddle around, 
any boy, given half a change and the 
company of his own sex, will achieve 
that status some day. 

The ancient Hebrews had a custom 
of moving boys from the women’s 
tents to the men’s at any early age. 
As a substitute for this wise operation 
you can’t do better than start with two 
weeks at Boys’ Camp. 

And any Mother, tears dried and 
cooking chicken for Son’s first night 
home, looks a lot better when only a 
square of print is attached to her 
apron strings.

AMONG 

OURSELVES 


John R. Latimer 


Some people seem to be born with 
camping in their blood . . . they take 
to Camp like a duck takes to water. 
John R. Latimer is such a person! 
President of the Ontario Camping 
Association and for twelve years the 
Director of Kilcoo Camp for boys, in 
Haliburton, John was born in Toronto 
in 1930. By way of education he 
attended Lawrence Park Collegiate, 
Victoria College and Lome Greene’s 
Academy of Radio Arts. His parents 
appeared to realize when he was still 
a youngster that camping was not just 
an “extra” with John, but rather some¬ 
thing that was an integral part of his 
very existence. 

I well remember running across him 
at Kilcoo when he was seven or eight 
years of age. Turning to me he said, 
“You know, Chief, someday I’m going 
to be a C.I.T. and a Counsellor at this 
Camp”, and not many years later he 
was saying, “someday l r m going to own 
this Camp!” As the years rolled by he 
was not only a C.I.T., a Counsellor, 
and Waterfront Director, but also a 
Section Director, and then the Director. 

As a Camper 

Several things made a lasting impres¬ 
sion on me as I watched John as a 
Camper. The first was his enthusiasm 


By C. F. Plewman, 

Past President 

Ontario Camping Association 


and smiling countenance. Somehow 
Camp seemed to be just his cup of tea. 
The second was his unfailing tidiness, a 
trait that has carried over into the tidy 
kind of camp he now operates. Some¬ 
times when there is a change of leader¬ 
ship, a camp experiences a real break 
with the past. It was not so when John 
took over. His 17 seasons at Kilcoo had 
made him a real part of the camp. He 
did bring with him an added zest for 
camping, and particularly an awareness 
of the worth of each individual. 


As a Camp Director John has had 
many things going for him. His natural 
a flection for boys has won a big place 
for him in their hearts. His pleasant 
personality has captured the confi¬ 
dence and loyalty of the parents, and as 
for the staff, his sincerity and above all 
his understanding, brings out the best 
in each one of them and results in 
happy relationships and a job that is 
well done. 

It was no accident when one of the 
parents of a camper years ago, offered 
to stake John, should he decide to buy 
Kilcoo. Nor is it surprising that secur¬ 
ing campers is one of the least of John’s 
problems. Some years he has turned 
down enough registrations to have 
made another good sized camp. 

A Dream Come True 

It was a fall day in 1955 when John 
finally made good his promise to “some¬ 
day own this Camp”. Five years later 


40 


Canadian Camping 



lie and his wife completed the financial 
arrangements with his partners, so that 
now the Latimers have full ownership. 
Fantastic as it was, his boyhood dreams 
had conic true. 

No story about John Latimer would 
be complete without some reference 
to his wife Peggy. Peg is a Camp 
Director’s dream of what a good 
Director’s wife should be. No matter 
what the situation demands she seems 
equal to the occasion. It matters little 
whether it is running a buffet for 600 
on Visitors Weekend, overseeing the 
commissariat department, acting as 
postmistress or driving the truck during 
Advance Camp. Though the staff over¬ 
run their living room, she remains her 
placid and patient self and to all and 
sundry displays a genial personality and 
a kindly and often motherly interest. 
To know what helps John click, you 
have got to know Peggy. 


The Latimers have three children. 
David 6, Jeffrey 5 and Michael 2. No 
one needs to tell them how a parent 
feels about his child. 

John’s main hobby seems to be “life 
itself”. Maybe that is why he is 
interested in politics. I, for one, hope 
that he won’t get too involved too soon 
. . . the more camping has his undivided 
attention, the happier I will be. 

John has always believed that every 
child has an inherent right to a happy 
and rewarding Camp experience. That 
being so it was natural that he should 
play an important role in the life of the 
Ontario Camping Association. During 
the past twelve years he has been 
Treasurer, Public Relations Chair¬ 
man, and three times Chairman of 
the important Conference Committee, 
National Chairman of Centenary Jour- 

more page 55

CAMPING 

AND 

LEISURE 


By Prof. Kirk W ip per 


The world of today, in its pheno¬ 
menal technological progress, has intro¬ 
duced to man a wide range of new 
problems which have either directly or 
indirectly produced stresses beyond 
what may be described as normal. It is 
an age when the machine and its 
master, the clock, have seized control 
of man almost from the moment of his 
birth. Not only has technology with all 
its automated innovations made a 
dramatic entry to the scene, but other 
major factors are exerting their influ¬ 
ence as well. The population explo¬ 
sion, transportation and communication 
advances, alterations in family and 
social class status, depletion of natural 
resources and the stealthy arrival of a 
new leisure have all assumed significant 
roles on the stage of our society. It 
would be useful to discuss all of these 
but my particular concern here is with 
leisure. 

A Much Discussed Topic 

Leisure has relatively recently be¬ 
come a much discussed topic but it is 
by no means new. In both Greek and 
Latin the word for leisure is the English 
word for school. In the period of the 
golden age of Athens, only the favoured 
classes were educated because only they 
had leisure. They had freedom to do 
what they wanted to do. History has 
passed down to us the glorious results 


ol that period when leisure was under¬ 
stood and accepted. Unfortunately, 
vestiges of the notion that leisure 
belongs to the favoured classes still 
persists but such a restrictive attitude 
is a very superficial appreciation of the 
facts. The prognosis is that leisure will 
become more and more available to the 
masses who are least prepared for it. 

Generally western man, who has 
been absorbed by the industrial giant, 
has come to regard leisure in work 
terms — as diversion from his working 
hours, as “not- work” time. This idea 
is not synonymous with the concept of 
leisure as freedom from the necessity 
of being occupied. And this is a logical 
conclusion. It is extremely difficult in 
a work oriented society to think in 
terms other than work. 

And so leisure is suspected. Because 
it is the antithesis of virtuous work, 
it is the time when that amoral, 
unprincipled idea of play is carried on. 
There is then, a sense of uneasiness— 
of guilt about this— because leisure is 
equated with a lack of purpose to life. 
It was refreshing to note a plea for 
play in the American Pavilion at 
Expo, 1967. Here was an attempt to 
portray the importance of play in a 
society taken over by work-focussed 
industrialism. * 

Consequently, as Sebastian de Grazia 
suggested, man tends to work in his 
“not-work” time. He moonlights: he 
works on his vacation; he works at his 
sports; he takes on endless chores, club 
projects and frenzied tours. He does 
all this so he can get “things.” More 
work means more money which means 
more things. The Indian apparetnly 
was not the only one taken in for a 
bundle of trinkets. Again as Sebastian 
de Grazia has pointed out, “Man has 
been sold a life of quantity in the 
mistaken belief that he was getting 
quality.” 


42 


Canadian Camping 


The Slave of Time 

With all his determination to work, 
man has become the slave of time. He 
has become what is described as a 
transmitter and receiver of time. Time 
then is something to be saved, spent, 
earned and even to be worshipped. 

But leisure cannot and must not be 
entangled and confused with work or 
time. It should also not be equated 
with free time. No shortening of the 
work week, no time saving gadgets 
will turn free time to leisure. In free 
time it is possible and useful to exper¬ 
ience amusement, rest and recreation. 
These are not, however, the essence of 
leisure. When we tear ourselves away 
from the tyranny of the time machine 
and wrench ourselves free from the 
work ethic we can begin to talk of 
leisure. Again from de Grazia, “Free 
time is the gate and outside the gate is 
freedom.” Leisure is freedom to do 
what one wants to do. It is true that 
the machine has given us free time but 
it cannot bestow leisure. That we must 
create ourselves. 

Leisure then should be regarded as 
steeping oneself in the whole of 
creation, a state of being in which you 
pause and open yourself up to life — 
an unlocking of your mind and spirit. 
“Not to devour life but to delight in 
it” is the opportunity offered through 
leisure. It is not so much what is done 
in leisure, but how it is done that 
counts. Aristotle described leisure in 
one of his writings “A man will live 
thus, not to the extent he is a man, 
but to the extent that a divine principle 
dwells within him.” 

Because leisure was so highly prized 
by the Greeks, its misuse was held in 
disdain. The word acedia described 
such an abuse and interpreted means 
spiritual torpor, a deadly sin. 

Reaction to Leisure 

Flow does modern man tend to react 
to the prospect of leisure? His first 


reaction is fear — fear of boredom 
because he is unprepared. After all he 
has been completely preoccupied with 
work, the machine and the clock. He 
paradoxically appears to look forward 
to retirement but at the same time is 
apprehensive about it. He has hoped 
throughout his life to find adventure, 
diversion and worth and he is not 
certain that he has either found it or 
will find it in work. The question is, 
will he somehow find it in leisure? 

It will take time for our society to 
recognize the real difference between 
leisure and work — a first and significant 
step. Work may do many things for 
man including making him rich, but it 
is leisure that will perfect him. 

As leisure performs to a cool and 
wary audience, camping stands in the 
orchestra pit with an excellent script to 
assist the actor. Camping has a special 
message to convey in its adopted pur¬ 
pose. It is intended to be child-centred 
which implies that programme ought 
to be manipulated to accommodate 
the needs and interests of campers. 
Secondly, the activities of camp ought 



The cover cut sketches the old log cabin at 
Cochrane Camp , by Nora daughter of the tate 
A. L. Cochrane , so well known in camping 
circles. 


Winter , 1968 


43 




in every way conceivable to be steeped 
in the natural environment allow¬ 
ing a continuous process of outdoor 
interpretation. This would indicate 
that experiences in wildlife, camp- 
craft, orienteering, outdoor living 
skills, creative arts and crafts using 
natural themes and materials, swim¬ 
ming, canoeing and wilderness travel 
by canoe or on foot should be 
deliberately cultivated and are the basic 
tools of camp leadership. 

An Unique Responsibility 

Education has the responsibility of 
perpetuating and enhancing wisdom 
and of assisting man in the process of 
adaptation to his changing environ¬ 
ment. Camping has a unique and 
special responsibility in the adaptation 
process which assumes special signifi¬ 
cance as man faces the opportunities 
inherent in leisure. In the camp set¬ 
ting, young people should then be 
surrounded with experiences in which 
they learn to express, create, serve, 
belong, be recognized, compete and 
participate in new experiences. 

Immediately it should be obvious 
that the camping movement has 
unusual opportunities and responsi¬ 
bilities in reference to leisure. It is in 
the natural environment that young 
people can find the essence of leisure, 
that is, provided that the philosophy of 
the camp in its natural habitat allows 


for that discovery. For in his flexible, 
impressionable years, the camper can 
be in a receptive attitude of mind 
which calls upon his singular greatness 
and uniqueness. This response can 
only emerge if leadership is aware 
and sensitive and has itself stepped 
beyond the portal of freedom to 
experience the vitality, beauty and tran¬ 
quility of leisure through the natural 
environment. 

If camping accepts the notion that 
its natural setting has special qualities 
in reference to preparation and under¬ 
standing of leisure, it would follow 
that it is necessary to ensure such an 
environment for future generations. 
It is indeed a moral obligation to 
guarantee the preservation of our 
natural heritage. Not only is it of 
inestimable value for the perfection of 
man in his leisure, but man’s very 
survival depends on the manner in 
which he strives to preserve his natural 
environment. 

There is indeed mounting evidence 
of a widespread disregard for the 
natural world of which man is an 
integral part, and yet it is in the 
wilderness reaches that man is both 
inspired and nourished. Our camping 
young people must be convinced that 
man’s survival is dependent on the 
care, maintenance and respect for the 
natural environment. Future resistance 


AVER 

LUMBER STORES 

"JOE BEAVER" A GOOD JOE TO KNOW 

MORE THAN 285 STORES ACROSS CANADA 
FREE ESTIMATES AND PLANNING HELP 




44 


Canadian Camping 




to careless manipulation of natural 
areas will only be effective if a large 
section of our population becomes 
genuinely concerned about matters 
relative to such environments. To 
be aware it is necessary to be exposed 
and to be exposed may mean eventually 
to care. 

The stress on what might be called 
living space is intense and it will 
increase. It was suggested earlier 
that pressures of increasing population, 
advancing industrialization, improving 
channels of trasportation, must inevi¬ 
tably take their toll on the remaining 
natural islands of freedom and inspira¬ 
tion. Man listens for the call of the 
wild, but even as he listens it is vanish¬ 
ing or being pressed back into a 
crowded, uncomfortable corner. And 
yet something goes wrong with man 
when he cuts himself off from the 
natural world. He begins to search for 
substitutes through flower beds, small 
gardens, and a great variety of pets. 
Still he concedes that the out-of-doors 
is and always will be an opportunity 
for man to become acquainted with his 
noblest dreams. It is a place where 
leisure can blossom. 

In conclusion, camp leaders can 
undertake at least the following positive 
steps in recognition of the implications 
of leisure: 

— Assist youth to understand that 
leisure has a special meaning which 
can probably be best understood in 
and through the natural environment . 

— provide experiences which will help 
campers to adapt to a changing 
world in which leisure is an integral 
part , and in the process of adaptation 
to experience diversion y worth and 
adventure. 

— allow campers freedom to think , to 
write y to converse , to play , to create , 
to understand and to acquire what¬ 


ever skills are necessary to make 
leisure meaningful. 

—inspire a respect and sensitivity for 
the natural environment so that it 
is protected and preserved as an 
important leisure resource for present 
and future generations. 

The wisdom of the world was mad¬ 
ness if, in teaching man how to subdue 
nature and transform the earth, it made 
men turn their back on life. Our task 
in camping is not to teach our campers 
about making a living but about how 
to live.

November 17 - 19.

tales from the Newfoundland outports, 
a view of the human clement in camp¬ 
ing combined to make a success of the 
first Atlantic Provinces Regional Camp 
Directors’ and Administrators’ Semi¬ 
nar. Delegates came from places such 
as Killdevil Camp out of Corner 
Brook, Nfld., Charlottetown, Frederic¬ 
ton, Halifax, Grand Falls, Moncton, 
St. John’s. They represented the Angli¬ 
can Church, the Baptist Church, the 
United Church, YMCA’s, Girl Guides, 
Boy Scouts, Boys’ Clubs. One repre¬ 
sentation that might be regarded as 
unique was from a camp run by the 
Co-op Services, the 4H Clubs, and the 
Zionist Organization — eighteen men 
and women in all. 

Ross Seaman, immediate past presi¬ 
dent of the English Section of the Que¬ 
bec Camping Association, was the 
resource person for the group. The 
theme emphasized the “Human Rela¬ 
tions Aspect in Camping”. There were 
discussions on the Role of Leadership, 
Selection of Leadership, Methods of 
Measurement in Camping, Group 
Function, and Methods of Evaluation.

CREATIVE BEHAVIOUR 


“Creative Behaviour Guidebook'’ 

by Sidney J. Parries has been reviewed 
with such quality and insight by Jean 
Darrach of the Editorial Committee 
that we are presenting it as an article. 


Before 1950 there was not much 
worrying done, at least in print, about 
what was happening to the creative 
abilities of students in the overcrowded 
school systems of North America. Some 
psychologists like J. P. Guilford were 
aware of the problem and gave it a 
chapter here and there, but no one 
then offered ordinaiy teachers a clear 
idea of the nature of creativity. The 
various “progressive” or “free expres¬ 
sion” systems were said to develop 
creativity, but no effective tests existed. 

Under Achievers 

In the years since 1950 the increas¬ 
ing application of science to the 
processes of production have made it 
imperative to find out why some intel¬ 
ligent people are imaginative and 
ingenious, and others equally intel¬ 
ligent seldom initiate or invent any¬ 
thing. Most modern researchers seem 
to be testing the hypothesis that 
creative talents are quite widespread 
but that they are smothered, atrophied 
and cut off in our socializing and 
educational process in which the 
emphasis is all on conformity. They 
suggest the world is probably full of 
“creative under-achievers”. At a recent 
conference of recreationists in Toronto, 
Professor Alan Klein told his audience 
they paid only lip service to creativity; 
the truth was they “really hated 
creative kids” who made them uncom¬ 


fortable and disrupted all their plan¬ 
ning. The response of the group 
suggested that he had flicked a tender 
spot. 

In recent years publications on the 
subject of creative behaviour have 
appeared in such numbers that it is 
difficult to keep up with them. There 
is growing evidence that teaching tech¬ 
niques based on the current analyses 
of creativity do produce permanent 
improvement in the ability of students 
to do original thinking. A majority of 
the studies are based on experience 
with adults, but much work is being 
done with school children -and the 
next year or two should see the 
publication of results. 

Their Own Periodical 

The creative behaviourists now have 
their own periodical, The Journal of 
Creative Behaviour, edited by a pioneer 
in the field, A. F. Osborn. An early 
number listed a bibliography of over 
4,000 items, and a further list of about 
1,500 will be required to bring the 
catalogue up to the end of 1966. 

A handy way to catch up with all of 
this, and to get some practical ideas 
of how the theories are applied, is to 
invest in Sidney J. Parnes “Creative 
Behaviour Guidebook” 300 pages and 
the Workbook that accompanies it. 
Price of each $2.65 (Charles Scribcr’s 


48 


Canadian Camping 






Sons, New York). In addition to a 
complete 16-session course, the theories 
are outlined and compared; there is an 
immense bibliography of the literature, 
lists of films and tapes, and a survey 
of current courses offered in education, 
industry and government in the U.S. 

The short course that Professor 
Parnes offers is one that he has been 
using and refining since 1956. It has 
the same air of being cut, dried and 
boxed up that programmed courses 
have — understandable since it is 
intended to be used for self-study as 
well as for seminar or workshop 
groups, but consorting oddly with 
the declared purpose of the material, 
to produce exciting, free-wheeling, 
creative thinking. Some of the “gim¬ 
micks” and exercises are no longer 
new, having made their way into 
popular magazine articles. 

However, Parnes emphasizes that 
discipline is an important element of 
training in creative behaviour, and 
that it requires effort and practice to 
overcome the mental set we have 
toward stereotyped responses. Osborn 
has put it this way: It is easy to under¬ 
stand creative behaviour principles 
intellectually, but extremely difficult 
to internalize them — to use them 
automatically in everyday life. 

The sessions of the course have such 
titles as: Recognizing the Real Prob¬ 


lem, Encouraging the Creative Process, 
Idea-finding, Making Unusual Ideas 
Useful, Making Snap Decisions, Crea¬ 
tive Problem-solving. In the introduc¬ 
tion, prospective students are told their 
self-confidence and motivation will 
improve; they will find life more excit¬ 
ing and challenging, become both more 
open-minded and more sensitive to 
others.

WALLACE FOKBIE 

INTERNATIONAL CAMPER 
1883 - 1967 

By ]. H. Ebbs, M.D., F.R.C.P.(C) 

Until his death on December 1, 1967, 
probably no camp leader was known 
by as many campers throughout the 
world as “Wally” Forgie. He was 
known as “Commodore” by the many 
young leaders who came under his 
influence in Canada from 1908 until 
1927. Many men knew him when he 
served five years overseas in the First 
World War with the Y.M.C.A. 

Boys work in Western Canada then 
occupied a number of years during 
which he conducted many canoe trips 
into the north-west. He was an asso¬ 
ciate of the late Dr. Hedley Dimock 
who was succeeded by Professor Charles 
E. Hendry. 

Y.M.C.A. boys work then took 
“Uncle Wally” to India where he 
pioneered in camping. In 1935 he built 
Camp Tonakela near Madras, which 
was officially opened by Mr. and Mrs. 
Taylor Statten. He then began thirty- 
two years of voluntary service to 
underprivileged children which has 
become an international project. 

At Camp Tonakela 

Camp Tonakela became an “oasis” 
on the plains to which thousands of 
orphans, blind and street children of 
Madras came for a few days of holiday 
in a North American style camp. Built 
around a well which provided water 
for trees and eventually a swimming 
pool, it was also an essential source of 
water for the families living in the 
surrounding villages. 

Gradually the services provided be¬ 
came known throughout the district 
and since the camp was fourteen miles 
from Madras which is the nearest 
source of medical help, Wally Forgie 
provided valuable free first-aid treat¬ 
ment to thousands of local people. 


The care and feeding of poor child¬ 
ren attracted convalescent children dis¬ 
charged from hospital with no home or 
source of care to go to. His reputation 
for good rehabilitation of sick children 
grew and this service is now an 
important part of the camp. 

Children from the surrounding vil¬ 
lages became a serious problem during 
several droughts and disastrous crop 
failures. Emergency one-meal-a-day 
feeding of these children has finally 
developed into a routine vitamin and 
mineral enriched daily meal for these 
neighbours. 

Wally Forgie, known as “Tah-Tah” 
by his Indian children friends, has 
demonstrated how one man can provide 
service to thousands of boys and girls, 
many many leaders and be an example 
to many fine Madras citizens who 
worked with him. As the head of the 
Child Health Institute of Madras has 
said “Wallace Forgie will be remem¬ 
bered in this part of the world as an 
Albert Schweitzer”. 

A Modest Man 

A modest, unselfish man with a 
practical missionary spirit, he would be 
the last to acknowledge that probably 
his greatest contribution has been his 
willingness to share his great humani¬ 
tarian venture with thousands upon 
thousands of campers in North America 
who have developed an awareness of 
the needs of others around the world. 
Wherever he went in the camps in 
Canada and the United States, he 
made friends as he told his simple story 
of a “North American Camp” at Camp 
Tonakela in India. 

Wally Forgie’s image will live on as 
a testimonial to his great work in camp¬ 
ing for the underprivileged, in camp 
leadership and in health service. It is 
to be hoped that support will be found 
for a tangible memorial to a fine 
‘camper’ at Camp Tonakela.

CANADIAN 
SYMPOSIUM 
on Recreation 

— A Summary — 

By Prof. Kirk Wipper 


The Symposium was held June 10 
to 16, 1967 at the Convention Hotel in 
Place Bonaventure in Montreal. The 
founding members adopted the title 
“Man and his Leisure” or “L’Homme 
au Loisir” in recognition of the Expo 
theme “Man and his World.” In the 
founding group were: Parks and 
Recreation Association of Canada; 
Association Canadienne des Centres de 
Loisirs; and the Recreation Division 
of the Parks Department, City of 
Montreal. 

The Symposium succeeded in draw¬ 
ing together the largest gathering of 
its kind ever assembled in Canada to 
deal with the subject “Man and his 
Leisure.” 

To accommodate the diversity of 
representation the Symposium explored 
a wide range of ideas through addresses, 
discussions and demonstrations. 

A Few Quotes 

A few relevant quotes may serve to 
indicate the scope of presentations. 

Hon. Allan J. Mac Ear hen, Minister of 
National Health and Welfare — “The 
quality of a society is determined by 
what it does with its leisure, its so-called 
non-productive hours.” 

Dr. Celeste Ulrich, physical education 
professor at the University of North 
Carolina—“We are moving away from 


the puritan ethic in North America that 
insists work is worth but play is passion 
and therefore shameful.” 

Dr. Wilder Penfield — “In our great 
democracy all men are free to discover, 
each for himself, an impelling purpose 
in life . . . when purpose comes, idleness 
is changed to opportunity. Leisure will 
then no longer pose a problem to the 
worker with a larger pay cheque and 
shorter hours of work.” 

Mr. Robert D. Freeze, lawyer and 
businessman of Vancouver—“Advertis¬ 
ing and promotion can create the desire 
to participate. It can demonstrate the 
benefit from participating and it can 
show how the activity can satisfy our 
social needs, our physical needs and 
our ego needs.” 

Hon. Arthur Laing, Minister of Indian 
Affairs and Northern Development — 
“We can no longer assume that Canada 
will always have enough countryside, 
suitable for any purpose we require . . . 
even in a country as vast as this we can 
use up our potential. . . . There is a 
need, deep within urban man com¬ 
pelling him to renew his communion 
with the world of trees, of sky and 
running water. Families need open 
places for children to meet the wonders 
of the natural world.” 

Lloyd Brooks, National Parks Service 
—“Providing for a quality environment 
on a national scale implies national 
leadership in these matters. There is 
evidence of the emergence of such 
leadership — (throne speech excerpt) 

. . . we must lose no more time in mak¬ 
ing ugliness in our environment as 
unwelcome as financial losses in our 
balance sheets.” 

To Conclude 

The Symposium, resolutions were 
drafted. These seemed to reflect the 
following summary statements which 
could have some influence on the future 
of camping.

Our Good Wishes 

to 

JOHN F. DALTON 

Last June, after forty years as an 
active member of the Quebec Camp¬ 
ing Association, Mr. John F. Dalton 
retired. Here is a gentleman who can 
look back with justifiable satisfaction 
at a substantial list of accomplishments 
in a number of areas of service. 

He was instrumental in establishing 
Boy Scout troops in various Catholic 
parishes throughout Montreal. It was 
he, also, who played an important part 
in establishing the Catholic Men’s 
Rehabilitation Centre, the Holy Cross 
Boys’ Club and the Victoria town Boys’ 
Club in that city. Mr. Dalton is a 
member of the Corporation of Pro¬ 
fessional Social Workers of his pro¬ 
vince, a member of the Boys’ Clubs 
Professional Association and of the 
Board of Directors with Boys’ Schools 
of Canada. 

He was a school teacher for 22 years 
and started work with the Federation 
of Catholic Charities in 1937. For over 
30 years he was the Executive Director 
of the Catholic Boys’ Services. 

Mr. Dalton’s camping interests, too, 
were inclusive. He was Chairman of 
the Membership Committee of the 
Quebec Camping Association and very 
capably handled the registrations at 
the 1962-64 and 1966 joint Confer¬ 
ences. In 1949 he established Trail’s 
End Camp. 

The best wishes of the Canadian 
Camping Association go to Mr. Dalton 
for whatever he now plans for future 
days; undoubtedly many people will 
continue to seek his counsel and draw 
upon his wide experience.

1. 7 he age of leisure is emerging in 
our society with every indication 
that it will shortly become a very 
significant force. 

2. 7 here is a growing awareness and 
readiness to respond to the implica¬ 
tions of leisure. 

3. There is a realization that, it will be 
essential for governmental bodies 
and private voluntary organizations 
to cooperate in facing the implica¬ 
tions of leisure. 

4. There is a recognition of the need 
to prepare leadership for leisure on. 
a very broad cooperative scale. 

5. There is a developing trend in each 
organization and institution con¬ 
cerned with leisure to re-evaluate its 
role in reference to leisure with the 
intent to retool , if necessary, toward 
a more effective contribution in the 
leisure field.

from p igc 46 

The Nova Scotia Camping Asso¬ 
ciation organized the conference and 
the Planning Committee included 
the Provincial President, Rev. David 
Hartry, Robert Cameron, New Bruns¬ 
wick liaison member of the N.S.C.A., 
David Mills, P.E.I. liaison member of 
the N.S.C.A., Ron lies of the N.S.C.A. 
Executive and myself. 

One of the most significant impres¬ 
sions derived from the conference was 
the need to share communication with 
camping people so that help and 
resources can be made available. This 
is particularly true where, as in the 
Maritimes, camping is predominately 
of an agency type and leadership 
is often transient and often non¬ 
professional. 

Camping is quite new in many parts 
of the Atlantic provinces and Camp¬ 


ing Associations exist only in Nova 
Scotia (10 years) and Newfoundland- 
Labrador (1 year). The need to 
disseminate information, resources, and 
support is felt to be a high priority in 
this area. I hope the Canadian Camp¬ 
ing Association will realize that the 
needs and action for resolving these 
concerns are quite different from 
those for the bigger, longer established 
Camping Associations. 

This conference may have provided 
the impetus — long needed — to bring 
about more communication between 
camping people and a sharing of 
common problems. Impetus may 
have been given, also, toward the 
strengthenting of existing Associations 
and maybe the development of Asso¬ 
ciations in New Brunswick and Prince 
Edward Island.

Sermons 

®iuber ®l)e H>un 

by Nairn Waterman, 
junior Leader Boys' Camp, 

July 31, 1960—Camp Wabanaki 

You all know the definition of 
courage. The dictionary gives one as 
‘bravery or fearlessness’. But courage 
has several meanings and some of the 
ones we think little about may be the 
more important ones. It takes many 
kinds of courage to go through life— 
the courage to face the facts, to solve 
problems, the courage to accept assign¬ 
ments, to stay with what we have 
started, the courage to follow through, 
the courage to preserve principles and 
sometimes fight for them and even the 
courage to run away. Many different 
kinds of courage which are not readily 
used in the home are necessary in a 
communal effort such as camp. 

One of these is subjection and 
obedience that we should gladly follow 
the counsel of others. That one word 
gladly takes a lot of courage in itself. 
We must sometimes set aside our own 
will though it seems good. I have 
heard it said several times that while 
we are young we sometimes wonder 
how our parents could be so stupid, 
but as we get older we wonder how 
they could learn so much in a few 
years. 

It takes courage to stick to a job and 
do it cheerfully. Some years ago the 
Norwegian Freighter Grontoft sank off 
Cape Race in a terrible hurricane. In 
the midst of the excitement attending 
the ship’s disaster, the ship’s wireless 
operator stuck to his post and filled the 
air with traditional S.O.S. calls for 
help. A liner picked up the message 
and started to make the rescue, 
signalling its progress as it came— 
4 miles per hour was the liners top 
speed, and the operator on board the 
Grontoft knew he would never arrive 
in time to effect a rescue. Bravely he 


kept on signalling. The Grontoft’s 
decks were awash; Death was a 
certainty. “This is no weather to be 
without an umbrella”, he checked to 
the rescuer and then shortly thereafter, 
“The stewards are making sandwiches 
for the lifeboats, it looks like we are 
going on a picnic.” He knew the life¬ 
boats could not live on such a sea, but 
he was going to be game and cheerful 
to the end. The next heard by the 
rescuers was the official report that the 
Grontoft was sinking. Then she heard 
the operators last message, “Sorry we 
couldn’t wait pressing business else¬ 
where”, and then he ended with the 
Norwegian toast “skol”. We probably 
will never have to stick to a job facing 
such high consequences, but everyday 
in camp we have little examples of 
this during cleanup or during skills, but 
always remember once you start a job, 
stick to it till the finish and do it as 
cheerfully as possible. 

Have you read the fable of the 
Philosophical clock, which one day 
meditated about its future? It had 
been bought in a store and placed on a 
shelf in a large farmhouse room. 
Almost at once it began to worry about 
all the work it had to do. It had to 
tick twice every second, that meant 120 
ticks per minute, or 72,000 ticks even’ 
hour, or 172,800 ticks every day. Each 
year it would have to tick 63,072,000, 
and in 10 years 630,720,000 times. 
Such thoughts were too much for the 
clock’s nervous system, and it passed 
out from the strain. 

But after it came to it had a flashing 
insight. It realized it had to tick onlv 
one tick at a time. This gave it a 
powerful injection of courage, so it 
went about its duty of ticking and has 
been at it for 25 years. Everybodv 
who lives on the farm counts on its 
faithfulness. Like the philosophical 
clock, we must realize we cannot get 
all things done at once. That we must 
face each job as it comes and finish 
that job well before we start another.
